newsitem.title: FRANCE: French take no chances with arms for Albania force.
newsitem.headline: French take no chances with arms for Albania force.

text.p: The French contingent in a United Nations-approved international force for Albania would pack a heavy punch to help discourage armed bands from preying on aid convoys, a senior officer said on Thursday.
"We're going to show our strength so that we don't have to use it," the officer told Reuters. "We're going in with helicopters, armoured personnel carriers and wheeled tanks,"

The officer was speaking after Defence Ministry spokesman Pierre Servent told reporters the multiplicity of weapons in the hands of what he said were "sometimes mafia-like bands," would be the main danger facing the force.

Servent said the French contingent, part of an Italian-led force of about 5,000 men, would be fully operational in Albania 10 days after receiving final orders expected to emerge from a planning meeting in Rome on Friday.
Advance units could be in Albania before then but the brunt of the contingent, including heavy equipment, would leave southern French ports by sea, he said.

The senior officer, who spoke separately, said the French contingent would be made up of mechanised marine units rather than paratroopers who move faster but were more lightly armed. The marines will be accompanied by combat engineers.
Designed to secure the distribution of humanitarian aid in the impoverished country, the force will be charged with securing the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport.
Servent said France wanted to handle the Durres area and the movement of supplies from there to Tirana.
"It is possible that some mafia-like bands along the way will want to grab some of the aid supplies so we will be on hand to prevent that.

"The problem is that tens of thousands of weapons are in the hands of the population and many Albanians know how to use them since the fallen Communist regime had a widely spread local militia organisation," he said.
Servent said the force would not specifically seek to confiscate weapons but this might happen if civilians opened fire on the international troops.
"Our mandate allows use to use force to carry out our mission. Anyone who tries to prevent us from doing so can be neutralised and his weapon taken away," he said.
Italy is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400. Servent said Austria had also offered troops.
Servent said France expected that a senior post in the international force, such as chief of staff to its Italian commander, would go to a French officer.
He said the south of the country "was a particular problem".

The revolt which broke out in Albania, prompted by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes, left thousands destitute and the south lawless for weeks, with groups armed with weapons looted from army depots roaming the area.

Rebel committees controlling southern towns say they are trying to stop the banditry and looting that has killed scores of people but demand the resignation of President Sali Berisha, blaming him for the collapse of the investment schemes.
